1. What DataSHIELD and OMOP mean

Source: vignettes/book-01-mental-model.Rmd
book-01-mental-model.Rmd

What you will learn

Distinguish the database, a private assignment and a released aggregate.

This chapter uses the synthetic practice connection from Getting started. Run the sections in order in one R session. All printed results below were computed with dsOMOP and dsOMOPClient 2.10.4. They are teaching data, not clinical findings.

A shared table structure

OMOP is a common data model (CDM): a shared set of tables and column meanings. person describes people; visit_occurrence describes visits; observation holds observations and questionnaire answers; death records deaths. A concept is a coded meaning, such as an education answer. A vocabulary supplies its name.

Ask which tables are available:

tables <- ds.omop.tables(conns = conns)
tables$site
#>            table_name schema_category has_person_id concept_prefix
#> 1              person             CDM          TRUE           <NA>
#> 2  observation_period             CDM          TRUE           <NA>
#> 3    visit_occurrence             CDM          TRUE          visit
#> 10        observation             CDM          TRUE    observation
#> 11              death             CDM          TRUE           <NA>
#> 27         cdm_source             CDM         FALSE           <NA>
#> 28            concept      Vocabulary         FALSE           <NA>
#> 29         vocabulary      Vocabulary         FALSE           <NA>
#> 35   concept_ancestor      Vocabulary         FALSE           <NA>

These are table names, not records. You can learn the structure without seeing a person’s dates or answers.

Send a question to the data

DataSHIELD sends approved operations to the server. An assignment creates a private object there. An aggregate returns a checked summary. The server can refuse a result that lacks enough supporting people; a refusal is not a zero.

Ask for safe information about the person table:

ds.omop.table.stats("person", conns = conns)$per_site$site
#> $rows
#> [1] 20
#> 
#> $persons
#> [1] 20

Read the reported count bands as bands, not exact counts. A later categorical table may release exact supported cells through its own checks. Different endpoints answer different questions and have different disclosure rules.

What stays on the server

You never download this book’s assigned person table through DataSHIELD. person_id becomes a pseudonym, but pseudonyms are still private row values. Dates and ages are also private. Coarsening dates helps define a useful analysis; it does not grant permission to fetch rows.

The practical sequence is: choose events, describe variables, assign a table, then request an aggregate. Chapters 5–7 walk through it one small step at a time.

Recap

OMOP makes data structures familiar. DataSHIELD keeps patient rows at the server and checks released summaries.

Try it

Find the columns of the death table without asking for its rows.

Solution

ds.omop.columns("death", conns = conns)$site
#>             column_name cdm_datatype db_datatype      concept_role semantic_class
#> 1             person_id      integer     integer       non_concept       ordinary
#> 2            death_date         date        text       non_concept       ordinary
#> 3 death_type_concept_id      integer     integer      type_concept        concept
#> 4      cause_concept_id      integer     integer attribute_concept        concept
#>      fk_domain is_date is_extension is_untyped_identifier is_sensitive is_blocked
#> 1                FALSE        FALSE                 FALSE        FALSE      FALSE
#> 2                 TRUE        FALSE                 FALSE        FALSE      FALSE
#> 3 Type Concept   FALSE        FALSE                 FALSE        FALSE      FALSE
#> 4                FALSE        FALSE                 FALSE        FALSE      FALSE
#>   is_quasi_identifier
#> 1               FALSE
#> 2                TRUE
#> 3               FALSE
#> 4               FALSE
